name: Arcs Designer Diary 3 - The Trick's the Thing (Leder Games)
one_line: Cole Wehrle's diary on why Arcs uses trick-taking as its core action-selection system, explicitly to fight the multiplayer-solitaire tendency of Eurogames
take_what: Lead/Follow action economy: on your turn you either play a HIGH card to seize the lead action (fewer total actions that round) or a LOW card to let someone else lead but you and everyone get MORE actions - the whole table is forced to react to whichever card the leader shows, every single turn, because it decides what action is even available that round

name: Arcs Designer Diary 3 - face-down copy & initiative-steal rules
one_line: Same diary - the specific fallback rules that keep losing players engaged instead of shut out of the round
take_what: A player who can't/won't fight for the lead can play their card FACE DOWN to copy a weakened version of the current lead action (still participates, still relevant); any player can also burn an extra card to seize the lead outright mid-round at the cost of skipping their own action later - both keep every player making a live decision on every other player's turn, not just their own

name: Why Race for the Galaxy is definitely not multiplayer solitaire (BGG thread)
one_line: BGG thread defending RftG against the multiplayer-solitaire charge via its simultaneous role-selection system
take_what: Every round all players secretly pick 1 of 7 roles and reveal simultaneously; ALL selected roles fire for EVERYONE that round, but only the player(s) who picked a given role get a bonus on it - so your choice of role is a bet on what your opponents will pick, and picking a role your opponent needs denies them the bonus even though they still get the base action
constraint: role-selection is a genre staple, easy to reimplement as a mechanism not IP

name: Stately Play review of Race for the Galaxy
one_line: Review that names RftG's low-interaction reputation directly and frames it as a design-philosophy tradeoff (racing to build vs. attacking)
take_what: Reviewer's framing that a game can be legitimately low-interaction if it fully commits to being a RACE (relative standing matters, not board presence) - names the exact tension Limen is trying to avoid: 'racing to build the best engine rather than blowing each other up'

name: Multiplayer Solitaire? (BGG Mechanica thread)
one_line: General BGG discourse thread on what makes engine-builders feel like multiplayer solitaire
take_what: Community consensus framing: 'multiplayer solitaire' = each player optimizes their own board/engine without needing to track or respond to what opponents are doing - the diagnostic test is 'could you play this exact same turn if the other player's board were hidden from you?' If yes, it's solitaire
constraint: none - diagnostic heuristic, not a mechanic to port

name: Wingspan solo-vs-multiplayer criticism (Table for ONE review)
one_line: Review naming Wingspan as a 'classic example of multiplayer solitaire' with near-zero cross-player interaction
take_what: Named failure mode: the ONLY interaction point in Wingspan multiplayer is card-sniping (someone takes the bird you wanted from a shared row) - everything else (egg-laying, food, bonus cards) is purely internal to your own tableau. This is the anti-pattern Limen's 'own corner' problem resembles: interaction reduced to a single shared-resource contention point instead of woven through the whole turn

name: Splendor rules - shared card row + token pool
one_line: Splendor's shared 4-card-per-tier display and shared communal token pool as the sole interaction surface in an otherwise parallel-building game
take_what: Only 4 cards per tier are ever face-up and purchasable at once, drawn from a shared deck - so a card you're saving up for can be bought out from under you by anyone, anytime, forcing a live threat-read every turn ('do I buy now at a loss, or risk losing the tempo play'). Same for gem tokens: taking 2-of-a-color requires 4+ remaining, so hoarding denies opponents outright
constraint: none - shared-limited-display is a generic mechanism

name: Dominion attack cards (Witch/Militia/Curse) design intent - Simulate Dominion blog
one_line: Analysis of Dominion's attack-card subsystem, the mechanism most credited with making an otherwise-parallel deckbuilder feel competitive
take_what: Attack cards (Witch gives opponents a dead Curse card that clogs their deck and costs -1VP; Militia forces opponents to discard down to 3 cards) are OPTIONAL cards in the shared market, not baseline rules - so interaction level is a dial the table sets by which market cards get included that game, and a Moat-type reaction card lets a target cancel the attack, creating a rock-paper-scissors tension around whether to invest turns in defense
constraint: Dominion's specific cards are IP; the 'attack cards are optional buy-in, defense is a purchasable counter' pattern is generic

name: Board Game Design Day: "King Me" - A Defense of King-Making (GDC Vault)
one_line: GDC talk defending king-making (a losing player's choice deciding who wins) as a legitimate, even desirable, interaction mechanism rather than a bug to design out
take_what: Reframes 'kingmaking' - normally considered a flaw - as evidence a game has REAL interaction: if a losing player's final moves can swing the outcome between two leaders, every player's position matters to every other player until the very end, which is the opposite of parallel solitaire play where only your own score matters
constraint: talk video, not fully transcribed by fetch - treat as pointer for deeper viewing

name: Best Multiplayer Engine Building Games with High Player Interaction (BGG thread)
one_line: Crowd-sourced list of engine-builders players consider genuinely interactive, as a counter-reference set
take_what: Existence of a whole BGG genre-request thread confirms 'interactive engine-builder' is treated as a rare, sought-after subcategory, not the default - validates that Limen's problem (interactive tile/engine game) is a known hard design target worth solving explicitly rather than assuming genre conventions handle it
